items.originalTitle: Democrats have reached a détente in their internal war. Will it last?
items.author: Lisa Kashinsky
items.title: Democrats have reached a détente in their internal war. Will it last?
items.summary: Democrats’ long-warring ideological factions have reached a détente, new POLITICO Poll data shows . It may not last. Half of progressives and moderates now say the party is “somewhat” or “much more” unified since the election, according to the latest survey, conducted last weekend by PF Global. And everyone agrees on what the Democratic-led Congress needs to do first, above anything else: bring down the cost of living. The size and sweep of Democrats’ midterms romp appears to have temporarily quelled the electability questions that fueled the long-running standoff between the party’s factions. Progressives flipped House districts and snagged Senate seats on plainly purple turf. Many moderate candidates flipped deep-red territory for the first time in decades. Put together, Democrats are now headed for their biggest House majority of the century. “We’ve got this great big-tent party that’s coming into Congress, and I think that’s what people want,” said Pete Giangreco, a veteran Democratic strategist who worked across House, Senate and gubernatorial races this past cycle. “They don’t want these ideological divisions” Today, two out of three Democratic midterm voters believe that progressives make their party stronger — considerably higher than the 41% who said so before Election Day, according to polls taken before and after the midterms. Among self-described moderate Democrats, that belief has risen 26 points, from 33% to 59%. Among progressives, it’s risen from 58% to 74%. “If people are spending more time going after other Democrats instead of figuring out how to work together as a team, then I'm not sure that they've got the right priorities,” moderate Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) told POLITICO. But it’s not clear how long the unity will last. The polling reveals cracks are already starting to reemerge within Democrats’ coalition, foreshadowing potential intraparty fights to come on Capitol Hill and beyond into 2028. Democrats agree on the broad strokes of their priorities, but they diverge on the scope of lawmakers’ approach and the kind of presidential nominee they’d like to see. “Democrats, they don’t need to be getting too big-headed about this quote-unquote blue wave or blue tsunami,” said incoming Arizona 6th District Rep. JoAnna Mendoza. “What they need to focus on is making sure that we’re bringing people relief and that we’re taking action because that’s what people need right now.” The poll bears out two of Democrats’ near-universal takeaways from last Tuesday that are already shaping the shadow 2028 presidential primary: Voters want to elect fighters — and they want them to cut down high costs. The overwhelming majority of Democratic midterm voters — 78% — say bringing down the cost of living should be Democrats’ top focus as they come into control of Congress next year. Nearly as many, 71%, of Americans said the same. But Democratic voters internally disagree on approach. The POLITICO Poll data shows 47% of the party’s midterm voters prefer the next Congress’ agenda be set by Democrats who want major systemic reforms and government intervention to reduce inequality, compared to 39% who prefer Democrats who want pragmatic and targeted economic solutions. A majority of progressives, 57%, choose systemic reform. Moderates, meanwhile, are split between systemic reform (43%) and targeted economic solutions (44%) Those splits are poised to spill onto the presidential campaign trail. Even as voters broadly agree on wanting a “fighter” candidate, half of progressives still think someone with their ideology would be among the most electable in 2028, while just over a third of moderates, 36%, say someone in their lane has the best shot. Several possible White House aspirants are trying to push a public truce, arguing that factional infighting needs to take a backseat for now . "I don't think any voters think about it that way," Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro told reporters when asked by POLITICO whether there was a progressive or moderate takeaway from the midterms at Crooked Media's post-election conference in D.C. "People want to see the results of their government because whether you voted for Trump or Harris in the last election, your prices are still too damn high." Progressive Rep. Ro Khanna, in a post-election interview, said “we had electability across the board” in the midterms and that the question heading into 2028 is “who has the best vision for America.” Lauren Fedor contributed to this report.

items.originalTitle: Meet the 27-year-old behind the protein ad that helped flip Mississippi
items.author: Erin Doherty
items.title: Meet the 27-year-old behind the protein ad that helped flip Mississippi
items.summary: You know you’ve made a good ad when it’s outperforming an endorsement video from Barack Obama. Ryan Sayles, a 27-year-old Mississippi content creator, is behind arguably the best political spot of the election cycle: Democrat Scott Colom’s viral “ pick another protein ” ad against GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. You’ve probably seen it by now. The ad featured Mississippi voters’ blunt reactions to Hyde-Smith’s suggestion that people struggling with rising beef prices choose from other protein options. “Pick another protein? Shiiii-, I’d rather pick another senator instead.” “Pick another protein? She done lost her damn mind. I’d rather pick another senator.” Sayles was at his nephew’s football game when he realized something extraordinary was happening. “I was looking at the first numbers when it first dropped, and I was like, ‘Oh, this is about to be a really good video,’” he told POLITICO after Colom’s historic Senate race victory in the longtime Republican stronghold. “We had the Obama endorsement the day before, so that was our biggest video. It was like, ‘Dang, we ain’t ever gonna top that.’” “And then this ad came, and we posted it, and it outperformed anything we ever did,” Sayles said. The 30-second spot quickly became the talk of Mississippi and Washington, helping fuel Colom’s longshot campaign to unseat Hyde-Smith and become the first Black senator from the state since Reconstruction. And, it’s given Democrats across the country another blueprint for how to break through online ahead of a critical 2028 presidential race, as the party continues to rethink its strategy. With the ad — and Colom’s win — Sayles has gone from a newcomer who stumbled into campaigning almost by accident to a name to watch in Democratic digital politics, as the party looks for fresh ways to reach voters ahead of 2028. “[Sayles] should be considered the breakout-star of this cycle,” Colom wrote in a post on X about the viral ad earlier this month. “He’s going to be a giant in the media consultant game. He did GAME CHANGING work with SO little.” In an interview with POLITICO, Sayles described how his lack of prior political experience shaped his approach to creating the ad and why he thinks Democrats should listen more closely to the voters they’re trying to reach. He also discussed the unexpected attention he’s received since the ad — and why he hopes Colom’s victory will serve as a wake-up call for the party to invest in the South. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. How did you get involved with the Colom campaign? I did a lot of freelance videography and photography, and they really just needed a photographer for one event they were doing back in October. And I came and did video and pictures for him, and they kept me around. They were like, "Yeah, we need to work with him,” and then from then on, I never left. Take me behind the scenes of creating the protein ad. How did it come together? Scott and his brother, Andrew, along with [the] campaign manager Gerard, they all plotted the script together, and so they presented it to me. We filmed it, and I directed and made sure it [felt] like Mississippi. I guess I made it more Mississippi than what it was at the beginning. You know, [I] just added the entertainment or funny pieces of it, like emphasizing the way he said the words and stuff like that. And then I shot it, edited it, and added the music to it. I sat there and edited for like five hours. I've heard that man say “shit” a million times. Did you think it was going to go this viral? I had high hopes for it, but I just didn't know what it could do. A lot of our content was getting around Mississippi, but it wasn't getting around the country. Mississippians knew about Scott Colom’s content and what he was doing, but it wasn't nationwide — and I think that ad really put a national focus on what was brewing in Mississippi. Why do you think this particular ad took off so much and felt so natural? I think the reason it did well nationally is because I think a lot of people are fed up. A lot of times we don't express the way we feel, we hold it in, but I think this ad was an expression that people felt all around the country, that we just had the guts to put it out there. For Mississippi, of course it resonated because that's something we say down here. People say “shiiiit” all the time — like you know, that's the normal conversation. I think the best thing about the ad was it was centering people, centering voters ... You know, Scott was in the ad for about five seconds, but then that was the biggest ad of the cycle. I think it was just a lesson that people matter way more than politics. Did anybody worry the ad went too far? Do you think Democrats are sometimes too cautious? I think the dope part is, we didn't run that ad by anybody. … We didn’t go around getting OK’s from anybody ... we just put it out. But also … I've never worked on a campaign, and I think that I didn't have a sense of what Dems normally did. You know what I mean? We just did what we liked, and that was one of the big things Scott always talked about. “Man, if we are good with the content, we are good.” Scott is the best person I could’ve been in this situation with. He has been such a great person. He’s so creative, and he has allowed me to shine in ways that I just can’t believe. Did you hear from people in the Democratic Party after the ad came out? Like I said, this is my first campaign, so this is all a blur right now, honestly. But I would say that I've gotten messages, a lot of messages. I don't know who all those messages are tied to at this point, but I have gotten a lot of messages and people saying, “You did great work, we should talk.” I'm just happy. Mississippi is, we have hope again, man, that's the biggest thing. You know, this is my state. What could the Democratic Party learn from the Colom campaign’s digital strategy? I want to shout out my digital director. Lacy Nelson was the digital director, and she really helped turn things around when it came to just our distribution being able to put stuff out, because at first I was posting, taking pictures, filming, editing, doing everything by myself, and it was the worst headache. You gotta put your feet on the ground, you gotta understand the area in which you are working to try to get voters, and you gotta let them know that you see them and make them feel seen. You have to understand what resonates with people. People in Mississippi are not going to care about the things that somebody who lives in New York City cares about, it's going to be different. And that messaging needs to be different. You can't give Mississippi a New York message. Not that I'm an expert — like I said, this is my first campaign — but I think people should really focus on what that region is listening to. What does Colom’s victory mean for Democrats’ opportunities across the South? For a long time we’ve looked at it as impossible. And with very little resources, we showed that if you really get out and you do the work, you talk to people, you meet voters where they are, it is possible. Mississippi is one of the hardest places that could have happened. When you look at the investment and you look at what other places have received for that type of thing, it shows that the opportunity was always in Mississippi. … We just needed the investment, and I think that over the years, so many organizations have done the work to get us to this point, and we just seized the opportunity. There's real opportunity in the South. You just gotta invest.

items.originalTitle: Why BMI Is Not the Best Measure of Health
items.author: Alice Park
items.title: Why BMI Is Not the Best Measure of Health
items.summary: —Jupiterimages—Getty Images BMI, or body mass index, has long been a part of health evaluations. A calculation that takes into account a person’s weight and height, BMI is supposed to reflect how much excess fat a person might be carrying and give doctors a sense of a patient's risk for obesity-related health conditions. For years, however, doctors have found that BMI isn’t the best measure of obesity-related health, since it can’t distinguish between fat and muscle weight. In a study published Nov. 11 in Nature , researchers led by Francesco Rubino at King’s College London report that a new framework for assessing obesity that combines BMI with other measures can dramatically improve doctors’ ability to determine whether a person’s excess weight is a health concern or not. The study included more than a decade's worth of data from more than 844,000 people in China, Spain, the U.K., and the U.S. The scientists compared determinations of obesity calculated by either BMI alone or by the new combined framework, which includes BMI along with a person's waist circumference or their waist-to-height ratio. They found that using only BMI missed diagnosing obesity in nearly 9% of people and misdiagnosed 3% as having obesity when their body weight wasn’t an immediate reason for concern. The team used a model for comparing organ function in people without obesity to those with obesity to determine obesity-related health problems. They also tracked who died during the study. “The scale of the problem with BMI is beyond what we imagined,” says Rubino. “We all know that BMI doesn’t represent health accurately. But the scale of the problem is concerning because of the number of people it misclassifies, by misdiagnosing in both directions. This is dozens of millions of people in the large countries we studied, and across the world, we’re talking many, many more—so it’s really a concern.” Even when excess weight is correctly identified, not all experts agree on the appropriate next steps. The new framework, first proposed in 2025 by the Lancet Diabetes and Endocrinology Commission—which Rubino led—argues for a new classification called preclinical obesity, in which patients with excess weight do not necessarily require immediate treatment (or treatment at all). This condition, Rubino and others say, is distinct from clinical obesity, a medical diagnosis that requires more immediate interventions like diet, exercise, or drug options such as GLP-1 medications. In the current study, about 77% to 91% of people who had preclinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity over 10 years. In the study, about 5% to 11% of people in the general population were determined to have clinical obesity; their risk of dying during the study was 69% higher than people without excess fat. For those with preclinical obesity, the mortality risk was 19% higher than that of those without excess fat. Distinguishing clinical from preclinical obesity, therefore, “allows doctors to triage and treat people differently, because the two groups are meaningfully different and the difference in mortality is quite obvious,” says Rubino. “All in all, [the study results provide] quite a robust level of evidence to say that the old system of BMI is something that is unsustainable in the clinic.” Precision surrounding obesity diagnoses is even more relevant now that GLP-1 drugs can effectively treat the condition. Determining whether someone is already experiencing health-related issues in their organs could help doctors better counsel them about staying on these medications through the side effects, or it could inform their dosing decisions. “Obesity never had that kind of granular information diagnostically to deploy treatments proportionate to need,” says Rubino. The results should provide further support for shifting away from relying solely on BMI to assess obesity risk, says Rubino. In taking into account a number of related measurements, the new framework, he says, “is no different than the standards used to diagnose other conditions in medicine.”

items.summary: A district attorney in Kansas said he will not be pressing criminal charges against a woman who drove a pickup truck into spectators and bystanders on the sidelines of a youth soccer match last month. Two people were killed, including a 6-year-old. Tom Hanson has more.

items.originalTitle: ‘COPS’ camera crew captures deadly police shooting during New Mexico ride-along
items.title: ‘COPS’ camera crew captures deadly police shooting during New Mexico ride-along
items.summary: Video shows a foot chase and struggle after an officer stopped a man for jaywalking in Albuquerque. The crew ran for cover as gunfire erupted. The deadly shooting remains under investigation. NBC News’ Andres Gutierrez reports.
